title: Natural Language Processing
subtitle: From tokens and TF-IDF to n-grams, taggers, embeddings, transformers and large language models, classical and modern, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course in natural language processing covering classical and modern techniques: tokens, normalisation, stemming and Zipf's law; bag of words, TF-IDF, cosine similarity and edit distance; n-gram language models and perplexity; Naive Bayes text classification and evaluation; part-of-speech tagging with Viterbi, CKY parsing and entity extraction; word embeddings; recurrent networks, LSTMs, sequence-to-sequence models and attention; the transformer, positional encoding and subword tokenisers; BERT, GPT, prompting and sampling; and search with BM25, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation metrics and responsible NLP. Every chapter has Python labs verified in the built-in interpreter, plus an n-gram text generator and a self-attention explorer.

chapters.title: Text as data: tokens, normalisation and patterns

maps.title: Text basics
links: Corpus | is | A collection of texts
Token | is | A unit of text
Stopword | is | A very common word

summary: Natural language processing (NLP) lets computers work with human language. Text is first split into tokens (words, pieces of words or characters) and normalised: lower-cased, stripped of punctuation, perhaps reduced to stems or lemmas.
Counting words already reveals a lot, and Zipf's law says a few words are extremely common while most are rare.
Classical NLP is a pipeline of such steps; modern NLP learns many of them end to end, but tokenisation and data hygiene still matter.

glossary.def: A unit of text produced by tokenisation: a word, subword, punctuation mark or character.
A large collection of texts used for analysis or training.
Cutting off word endings by rule, so 'running' and 'runs' become 'run'.
Reducing a word to its dictionary form using vocabulary and grammar, so 'better' becomes 'good'.
A compact pattern language for matching text.

keyPoints: Tokenise, lower-case, remove noise.
Stem is a chopped root; lemma is a real word.
Zipf: frequency is about 1 / rank.
Out-of-vocabulary words are a problem for word-level models.
Subword tokens fix that.

items: ELI5. A computer cannot read. First we cut a sentence into little pieces, like cutting a sandwich into bites, and then we count the bites.
A tweet, a medical report, a legal contract, a novel: all are strings of characters. To compute with them we must decide what the pieces are. The first step is tokenisation.

In English, splitting on spaces and peeling off punctuation gets you far, but 'don't', 'New York', 'state-of-the-art' and a URL all raise questions. Languages without spaces, such as Chinese or Japanese, need other methods.

Normalisation reduces variation. Lower-casing makes 'The' and 'the' one word. Stripping accents, expanding contractions and fixing spelling help in some tasks and hurt in others: 'US' and 'us' are different.
Stopwords such as 'the', 'of' and 'and' carry little meaning for search and topic tasks and are often removed, though modern models keep them.

lesson.code:
import re, collections
text = 'The cats are running. The dog runs fast!'
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower())
print(tokens)
print(collections.Counter(tokens).most_common(3))

import nltk
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
print(PorterStemmer().stem('running'))          # run
print(WordNetLemmatizer().lemmatize('geese'))   # goose

items: Stemming and lemmatisation merge forms of one word. A stemmer such as Porter's chops suffixes by rules, so 'caresses' becomes 'caress' and 'running' becomes 'run', sometimes producing non-words like 'happi'.
A lemmatiser uses a dictionary and the part of speech to return real forms: 'geese' becomes 'goose' and 'better' becomes 'good'. Stemmers are fast; lemmatisers are more accurate.

Counting words reveals Zipf's law: the most frequent word occurs about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on, leaving a long tail of rare words, many appearing once.

This is why word-level vocabularies struggle with unseen words, and why modern systems split text into subword pieces. Regular expressions, patterns such as digits followed by a percent sign, remain the Swiss army knife for extracting dates, prices and codes.

chapters.title: Bag of words, TF-IDF and similarity

maps.title: Vectors
links: Bag of words | counts | Words per document

summary: The bag-of-words model describes a document by how often each word occurs, ignoring order. TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so words that are common everywhere count for little and distinctive words count for a lot.
Cosine similarity compares two document vectors by the angle between them, regardless of document length. Ranking documents by similarity to a query is the basis of classic search.
Edit distance (Levenshtein) measures how many insertions, deletions and substitutions turn one string into another, useful for spelling correction.

glossary.def: A representation of text as word counts, discarding order.
Term frequency times inverse document frequency; high for words frequent in a document but rare overall.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors; 1 means the same direction.
A vector with mostly zeros, as in bag-of-words with a large vocabulary.
The minimum number of single-character edits to turn one string into another.

keyPoints: tfidf = tf x log(N / df).
cos = a.b / (|a||b|).
Sparse vectors: store only non-zeros.
Query and documents in the same space.
Edit distance by dynamic programming.

items: ELI5. To find which book is about cats, count words, but ignore words like 'the' that every book has. The rare words tell you the most.

How would you find the document most about 'volcano' in a library of ten thousand? A first idea: count the word. But long documents win, and 'the' wins everything. TF-IDF fixes both. The term frequency, how often a word appears in this document, is divided by the length.
The inverse document frequency is the logarithm of the number of documents divided by the number containing the word. A word in every document has IDF zero; a rare, telling word has a large one.

lesson.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

docs = ['the volcano erupted', 'the cat sat on the mat', 'volcano ash covered the town']
vec = TfidfVectorizer()
X = vec.fit_transform(docs)
q = vec.transform(['volcano ash'])
print(cosine_similarity(q, X))

items: Each document becomes a vector with one position per vocabulary word. The vectors are huge and nearly all zeros, so we store them sparsely. To compare two vectors we use the cosine of the angle between them: the dot product divided by the product of their lengths.
Two documents using the same words in similar proportions point the same way, however long they are.

A search engine of this kind embeds the query as a vector too and ranks documents by cosine similarity, or by refinements such as BM25. It knows nothing about meaning: 'car' and 'automobile' share no dimension, so a query for one misses the other.
That limitation motivates the embeddings of Chapter 6.

A different kind of similarity is between spellings. The Levenshtein edit distance counts the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another: 'kitten' to 'sitting' is three. A table filled by dynamic programming computes it.
Spell checkers suggest the dictionary words within one or two edits of what you typed.

chapters.title: N-gram language models

maps.title: Language models
links: Language model | assigns | Probabilities to text
N-gram | conditions on | Previous n-1 words

summary: A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of words, or equivalently predicts the next word. An n-gram model assumes that the next word depends only on the previous n-1 words, and estimates probabilities by counting in a corpus.

Unseen word pairs would get probability zero, so we smooth: add-one (Laplace) smoothing, or back off to shorter contexts. Quality is measured by perplexity, the model's average surprise on held-out text; lower is better.
Language modelling is the idea behind autocomplete, speech recognition and, at a much larger scale, today's large language models.

glossary.def: A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words or predicts the next word.
A pair of consecutive words; a bigram model conditions each word on the one before.
Adjusting counts so unseen events get non-zero probability.
The exponential of the average negative log-probability per word; roughly the effective number of choices.
The assumption that the future depends only on a limited recent past.

keyPoints: P(w | prev) = count(prev w) / count(prev).
Add-k: (count + k) / (total + k V).
log P(sentence) = sum of log P(w | prev).
Perplexity = exp(-mean log P).
Larger n: more context, more sparsity.

items: ELI5. A phone guesses your next word by remembering which word usually came after the last one or two.

Your phone suggests the next word as you type. Behind it is a language model. 'I am going to' is often followed by 'be' or 'the' or 'bed', rarely by 'purple'. Language models turn that intuition into numbers.
The chain rule says the probability of a sentence is the product of each word's probability given everything before it. That is too much history to count.

The bigram model keeps only the previous word: the probability of 'sat' after 'cat' is the number of times 'cat sat' appears divided by the number of times 'cat' appears. Trigram models keep two words, and so on. This is the Markov assumption.

Counting has a trap. A perfectly good sentence may contain a word pair never seen in training, giving probability zero and, because probabilities multiply, probability zero for the whole sentence. Smoothing shares out some probability to unseen events. Add-one smoothing adds one to every count.
Kneser-Ney smoothing, which backs off to shorter contexts in a smarter way, was the best n-gram method for decades.

lesson.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import math

tokens = '<s> the cat sat on the mat </s>'.split()
bigrams = Counter(zip(tokens, tokens[1:]))
unigrams = Counter(tokens)
def p(w, prev, k=1, V=len(unigrams)):
    return (bigrams[(prev, w)] + k) / (unigrams[prev] + k * V)
print(p('cat', 'the'))

items: To judge a language model, compute how surprised it is by text it has not seen. The perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log probability per word. A perplexity of 100 means the model is as unsure as if it had to choose among 100 equally likely words at each step.
You can also run the model forwards: pick a next word from its distribution, append, repeat. N-gram generation gives locally sensible but globally rambling text, as the playground shows.

chapters.title: Text classification: Naive Bayes and sentiment
summary: Text classification assigns a label to a document: spam or not, topic, sentiment, language. A strong classical baseline is Naive Bayes, which combines the class prior with the likelihood of each word given the class, assuming words are independent.
Logistic regression or linear SVMs on TF-IDF features are usually stronger. Sentiment analysis can also use lexicons of positive and negative words, with care over negation.
Evaluate with held-out data and per-class precision, recall and F1, especially when classes are imbalanced.

glossary.def: A classifier that picks the class maximising prior times the product of word likelihoods, assuming conditional independence.
The probability of a class before seeing the document.
The probability of the words given a class.
Determining whether text expresses a positive, negative or neutral opinion.
The average of the F1 scores of each class.

keyPoints: class = argmax log P(c) + sum log P(w | c).
P(w | c) = (count + 1) / (total + V).
Work in logs to avoid underflow.
Negation flips polarity: 'not good'.
Macro F1 treats classes equally.

items: ELI5. To sort mail into 'happy' and 'sad' piles, count which words show up more in each pile, then vote.
Is this review positive or negative? Is this email spam? Which topic does this article belong to? Each is classification of text, and a simple method works surprisingly well.
Naive Bayes asks: given the label, how likely would the words be? Spam emails use 'free' and 'winner' more; ham emails use 'meeting' and 'attached'.
Bayes' rule turns this around. The probability of a class given the words is proportional to the prior probability of the class times the probability of the words given the class.
The naive assumption treats words as independent given the class, so the likelihood is a product of per-word probabilities. They are not independent, but the result ranks classes well.
Counting gives the probabilities; adding one to every count, Laplace smoothing, handles unseen words; working with logarithms avoids multiplying many tiny numbers.

lesson.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

clf = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2)), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
clf.fit(train_texts, train_labels)
print(classification_report(test_labels, clf.predict(test_texts)))

items: Sentiment analysis is a favourite task. A lexicon method adds up scores of words from a list: 'wonderful' plus two, 'dull' minus one. It is transparent but trips on negation, 'not good', sarcasm and domain: 'unpredictable' praises a thriller and damns a car.
Handling negation, for instance by flipping the score of words after 'not' until punctuation, fixes some mistakes.
Measure on data the model has not seen. Accuracy can mislead with imbalanced classes. Precision, recall and their balance, F1, per class, and the macro average of them show where the model fails.
Pre-trained transformers, which you meet in later chapters, now beat these classical models on most benchmarks, but Naive Bayes and logistic regression remain fast, cheap, explainable baselines.

chapters.title: Linguistic structure: tagging, parsing and entities
summary: Language has structure. Part-of-speech tagging labels each word as noun, verb and so on; context matters, since 'duck' can be either. A hidden Markov model with the Viterbi algorithm finds the most probable tag sequence.
A context-free grammar describes how phrases build sentences, and a parser recovers the tree, for example with the CKY algorithm. Dependency parsing links each word to its head.
Named entity recognition finds names of people, places and organisations, usually by tagging tokens with B-I-O labels.

glossary.def: The grammatical category of a word, such as noun, verb or adjective.
A model with hidden states (tags) that emit observed words and move by transition probabilities.
A dynamic programming method that finds the most probable hidden state sequence.
A set of rewrite rules such as S -> NP VP that generate sentences.
Finding and classifying names of people, organisations, locations and so on in text.

keyPoints: Viterbi: best[t][s] = max over p of best[t-1][p] T[p][s] E[s][w].
CKY fills a chart for spans.
BIO tags: B-PER begins, I-PER continues, O outside.
Dependency: each word has one head.
Neural taggers now give the best accuracy.

items: ELI5. A sentence has a shape. 'The' leads to a noun and a noun leads to a verb. A tagger finds each word's job by picking the likeliest path.

Read 'Time flies like an arrow' and 'Fruit flies like a banana'. The same words get different structures. Understanding language requires more than a bag of words. The first layer of structure is the part of speech. 'Flies' might be a verb or a noun, and neighbours decide.
A tagger assigns each word a tag using the surrounding words.

The classic model is the hidden Markov model. Tags are hidden states. Each tag tends to follow certain tags, determiner then noun, which gives transition probabilities, and each tag emits certain words, which gives emission probabilities.

Given a sentence, the number of possible tag sequences is huge, but the Viterbi algorithm finds the best one in time proportional to the length times the square of the number of tags, by keeping, for each position and tag, only the best path ending there.

Above tags sit phrases. A context-free grammar has rules such as a sentence is a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase, and a noun phrase is a determiner followed by a noun. A parser finds the tree that the grammar assigns to a sentence.

The CKY algorithm fills a triangular chart with every constituent for every span of words, working from short spans to long. Ambiguity, as in 'I saw the man with the telescope', produces several trees, and probabilistic grammars choose the likeliest.

lesson.code:
import spacy
nlp = spacy.load('en_core_web_sm')
doc = nlp('Apple is looking at buying a U.K. startup for $1 billion.')
for t in doc:
    print(t.text, t.pos_, t.dep_, t.head.text)
for ent in doc.ents:
    print(ent.text, ent.label_)   # Apple ORG, U.K. GPE, $1 billion MONEY

items: Dependency grammars take another view. Instead of nested phrases, each word depends on exactly one head word, with a labelled link such as subject or object, giving a tree of word-to-word arrows. Named entity recognition finds mentions of people, organisations, places and dates.

It is usually treated as tagging with BIO labels: B marks the beginning of an entity, I its continuation, O everything outside. Today these tasks are done by neural networks trained on annotated treebanks, and later chapters show how pre-trained transformers made them much more accurate.

chapters.title: Word embeddings: meaning as geometry

maps.title: Embeddings
links: Distributional hypothesis | links | Context to meaning

summary: You shall know a word by the company it keeps. Words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings. Counting co-occurrences and reducing the table to dense vectors gives word embeddings, in which similar words are close together.
Word2vec and GloVe learn vectors of a few hundred numbers. Cosine similarity finds neighbours, and directions encode relations: king minus man plus woman lands near queen.
Embeddings reflect the text they were trained on, including its social biases, which must be audited.

glossary.def: The idea that words used in similar contexts have similar meanings.
A dense vector of real numbers representing a word, learned from text.
Positive pointwise mutual information: how much more often two words co-occur than chance, floored at zero.
A word2vec training task: predict the context words around a given word.
A word not seen in training and so lacking a vector.

keyPoints: PMI = log P(w, c) / (P(w) P(c)).
Similar words, similar contexts.
Skip-gram pairs (centre, context) in a window.
king - man + woman is about queen.
Contextual embeddings replaced static ones.

items: ELI5. Put words on a map where words used in the same places sit close together. 'Cat' ends up near 'dog' and far from 'train'.

The bag-of-words view treats 'car' and 'automobile' as strangers. But they appear among the same neighbours: drive, road, engine, parked. The linguist J. R. Firth put it as a slogan: you shall know a word by the company it keeps.
If we describe each word by the words around it, similar words get similar descriptions.
Build a table with a row per word and a column per context word, counting how often they appear within a few words of each other.

Raw counts are dominated by common words, so replace them by pointwise mutual information, which asks how much more often the pair occurs than if the words were independent. Table rows are long sparse vectors.
Reduce them, for instance with singular value decomposition, to 100 or 300 dense dimensions, and you have embeddings.

Word2vec, from Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google in 2013, learns the vectors directly with a tiny neural network. In the skip-gram variant, the network reads a word and tries to predict the words in a window around it. Training pushes words that share contexts toward similar vectors.
With negative sampling, random wrong words serve as the contrast. GloVe fits vectors to the log co-occurrence counts. Both train in minutes on a laptop.

lesson.code:
from gensim.models import Word2Vec
sentences = [['the', 'king', 'rules'], ['the', 'queen', 'rules'], ['a', 'dog', 'barks']]
model = Word2Vec(sentences, vector_size=50, window=2, min_count=1, sg=1, epochs=50)
print(model.wv.most_similar('king'))
# with pretrained vectors:
# print(wv.most_similar(positive=['king', 'woman'], negative=['man']))

items: The resulting space has remarkable regularities. Differences between vectors capture relations, so the vector for king minus man plus woman lies near queen, and Paris minus France plus Italy lies near Rome.

But the space also absorbs the prejudice of its training text: 'doctor' sits closer to 'he' and 'nurse' closer to 'she'. Static embeddings give one vector per word, even for 'bank' of a river and 'bank' of money.
Chapters ahead replace them with contextual embeddings from transformers, which give each occurrence its own vector.

practice.title: Analogy
practice.intro: Write analogy(a, b, c, vocab, vectors): find the word (excluding a, b, c) whose vector is nearest by cosine similarity to vec(b) - vec(a) + vec(c). Return the word (first on ties).
practice.solution:
import math
def analogy(a, b, c, vocab, vectors):
    va = vectors[vocab.index(a)]
    vb = vectors[vocab.index(b)]
    vc = vectors[vocab.index(c)]
    t = [vb[i] - va[i] + vc[i] for i in range(len(va))]
    best = None
    bs = None
    for i in range(len(vocab)):
        if vocab[i] in (a, b, c):
            continue
        v = vectors[i]
        dot = sum([t[j] * v[j] for j in range(len(t))])
        s = dot / (math.sqrt(sum([x * x for x in t])) * math.sqrt(sum([x * x for x in v])))
        if bs is None or s > bs + 1e-12:
            bs = s
            best = vocab[i]
    return best

chapters.title: Neural sequence models: RNNs, LSTMs and attention
summary: A recurrent neural network reads text one token at a time, updating a hidden state that summarises everything so far. It can predict the next word, tag every word or encode a whole sentence.

Plain RNNs forget over long distances because gradients shrink; LSTMs and GRUs add gates that control what to keep. Sequence-to-sequence models use an encoder RNN and a decoder RNN for translation and summarisation.
Attention lets the decoder look back at every encoder state and focus on the relevant ones. It removed the bottleneck of squeezing a sentence into one vector and led directly to the transformer.

glossary.def: A network that processes a sequence step by step, passing a hidden state from one step to the next.
Long short-term memory: an RNN with gates that decide what to forget, write and output.
An encoder-decoder model that maps an input sequence to an output sequence.
A decoding method keeping the k best partial outputs at each step.
A mechanism that computes a weighted average of states, with weights depending on relevance to the current need.

keyPoints: h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b).
LSTM: forget, input and output gates.
Teacher forcing: feed the true previous token in training.
Beam search keeps top-k hypotheses.
Attention weights = softmax(scores).

items: ELI5. A reader who remembers the story so far can guess what comes next. The memory is a small bundle of numbers passed along word by word.
Language comes in order, so it is natural to process it in order. A recurrent neural network keeps a small memory, the hidden state, a vector.

At each step it reads the next word's embedding, mixes it with the old memory through a weight matrix, and squashes the result with tanh to produce the new memory. The same weights are reused at every step, so the network handles sentences of any length.

The trouble is long distance. Training adjusts weights by passing gradients back through all the steps, and multiplying many numbers below one makes them vanish, so the network cannot learn that the verb at the end agrees with the subject at the start.

The LSTM, from Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997, adds a cell state and three gates, learned numbers between zero and one that decide what to forget, what to write and what to reveal. The GRU is a leaner relative.

lesson.code:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras import layers
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    layers.Embedding(20000, 128),
    layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(64)),
    layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid'),
])
model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

items: For translation, the sequence-to-sequence model of 2014 uses one RNN, the encoder, to read the source sentence into a vector, and another, the decoder, to write the target one word at a time. At test time the decoder must choose words.
Greedy decoding takes the best word each step and can paint itself into a corner, so beam search keeps the k best partial sentences and extends them all.

Squeezing a long sentence into one vector was a bottleneck. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio proposed in 2014 that the decoder, at each step, look back over all encoder states and take a weighted average, with weights from a learned score of how relevant each source word is right now. This is attention.

It sharply improved translation and also produced pleasing alignment pictures. Within three years, researchers asked what would happen if attention were the only mechanism and the recurrence was thrown out. The answer was the transformer.

practice.solution:
import math
def attend(query, states):
    scores = []
    for s in states:
        scores.append(sum([query[i] * s[i] for i in range(len(query))]))
    m = max(scores)
    e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in scores]
    t = sum(e)
    return [round(v / t, 4) for v in e]

chapters.title: Transformers: self-attention, positions and tokenisers
summary: The transformer replaces recurrence with self-attention: every token compares its query with every token's key and takes a weighted average of their values. All positions are processed in parallel, which makes training fast on GPUs.

Because attention ignores order, positional information is added. Several attention heads run in parallel, followed by feed-forward layers, residual connections and layer normalisation, repeated in a stack of blocks.
Text enters as subword tokens, built by algorithms such as byte-pair encoding, which merges the most frequent adjacent pairs to make a vocabulary of tens of thousands of pieces.

glossary.def: A layer where each token's output is a weighted mix of all tokens' values, with weights from query-key similarity.
Several attention operations in parallel, each with its own projections, whose outputs are concatenated.
Extra information added to token embeddings so the model knows their order.
A mask that prevents a position from attending to later positions, used for left-to-right generation.
A tokenisation method that repeatedly merges the most frequent pair of symbols.

keyPoints: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V.
Block = attention + MLP, each with residual and norm.
Causal mask: position i sees positions up to i.
Sinusoidal positions: sin and cos at many frequencies.
BPE: merge most frequent pair, repeat.

items: ELI5. Instead of reading in a line, every word can glance at every other word and decide which ones matter to it. 'It' looks back at 'the animal'.

The 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' began a revolution. Its idea: let every token look directly at every other token. Each token produces three vectors from its embedding: a query, saying what it is looking for; a key, saying what it offers; and a value, the content to pass on.
The match between a query and each key, the dot product, scaled down by the square root of the vector length, is turned into weights by a softmax. The output is the weighted sum of values.

Compare with the RNN. A recurrent network passes information along a chain, so a word at the start reaches the end only through many steps. In self-attention any two tokens interact in one step, so long-range dependencies are easy.
And since no step waits for the previous one, a whole sentence is computed in parallel, which is why transformers could be trained on far more data than RNNs.

lesson.code:
import torch, math
def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))
    return torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) @ V

L = 5
causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(L, L))   # position i sees j <= i

items: Attention treats the input as a set, so a sentence and its scrambled version would look alike. Positional information fixes this.
The original paper added sinusoids of many frequencies to the embeddings; modern models rotate the query and key vectors by position-dependent angles (rotary embeddings) or learn the positions.

For text generation a causal mask blocks each position from seeing later ones, so the model can be trained to predict every next word in parallel. A full block adds a position-wise feed-forward network, a residual connection around each part, and layer normalisation.
Multi-head attention runs several smaller attentions side by side so each can specialise.
How does text become the model's input? Word-level vocabularies fail on rare words and typos; character-level sequences are too long. Byte-pair encoding splits the difference. Start with characters.

Count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent into a new symbol, and repeat tens of thousands of times. Common words become single tokens, rare ones split into pieces, and anything can be spelled with bytes.
The model never sees spelling directly, which explains odd failures such as counting the letters of a word.

practice.title: Scaled dot-product attention
practice.intro: Write sdpa(Q, K, V): for lists of vectors compute softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V where d is the vector length; return the output vectors rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Scores, softmax, weighted sum of values.
practice.solution:
import math
def sdpa(Q, K, V):
    d = len(Q[0])
    out = []
    for q in Q:
        sc = [sum([q[i] * k[i] for i in range(d)]) / math.sqrt(d) for k in K]
        m = max(sc)
        e = [math.exp(s - m) for s in sc]
        t = sum(e)
        w = [x / t for x in e]
        dv = len(V[0])
        o = [0.0] * dv
        for a in range(len(V)):
            for j in range(dv):
                o[j] = o[j] + w[a] * V[a][j]
        out.append([round(x, 3) for x in o])
    return out

practice.title: Causal mask
practice.intro: Write causal_mask(L): an L x L matrix of 1 where column j <= row i (allowed) and 0 elsewhere.
practice.solution:
def causal_mask(L):
    return [[1 if j <= i else 0 for j in range(L)] for i in range(L)]

practice.title: Masked softmax row
practice.intro: Write masked_softmax(scores, mask): softmax of the scores where mask is 1; masked positions get weight 0. Round to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def masked_softmax(scores, mask):
    vals = [scores[i] for i in range(len(scores)) if mask[i] == 1]
    m = max(vals)
    e = [math.exp(scores[i] - m) if mask[i] == 1 else 0.0 for i in range(len(scores))]
    t = sum(e)
    return [round(v / t, 4) for v in e]

practice.title: Sinusoidal positions
practice.intro: Write pos_encoding(pos, d): the sinusoidal position vector of even length d: for i = 0, 2, 4, ... the pair [sin(pos / 10000^(i/d)), cos(pos / 10000^(i/d))]. Return the flat list rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def pos_encoding(pos, d):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, d, 2):
        a = pos / (10000.0 ** (i / float(d)))
        out.append(round(math.sin(a), 4))
        out.append(round(math.cos(a), 4))
    return out

chapters.title: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and beyond

maps.title: Pretraining
links: Next token | predicts | Left to right

summary: Modern NLP follows pretrain then adapt. A transformer is first trained on huge text with a self-supervised goal, then fine-tuned or prompted for tasks. Encoder models like BERT read the whole text both ways and produce contextual embeddings, suited to classification and tagging.
Decoder models like GPT, Llama and Claude generate text left to right, one token at a time.
Scaling model size, data and compute improved quality predictably and revealed abilities such as in-context learning, where the model follows examples in its prompt.
Large models are further aligned with instruction tuning and human feedback so they follow requests helpfully and safely.

glossary.def: Training a large model on unlabeled data with a self-supervised objective such as predicting masked or next tokens.
Hiding some tokens and training the model to recover them from context in both directions.
Training the model to predict each token from the ones before it.
Performing a new task from instructions and examples given in the prompt, without weight updates.
Further training so the model follows instructions, using demonstrations and human preference feedback.

keyPoints: Encoder: BERT, bidirectional, masked LM.
Decoder: GPT, Llama, Claude, causal LM.
Fine-tune with a small labelled set.
Prompt: instructions plus examples.
Temperature, top-k and top-p control sampling.

items: ELI5. First read a library of books to learn the language. Then a little extra practice makes the reader good at one job, like sorting reviews.

Before 2018, each NLP task trained its own model from scratch on its own small labelled dataset. Then came a new recipe. Pretrain one large model on enormous amounts of plain text using a goal that needs no labels, then adapt it to each task cheaply.
This is transfer learning, as in vision, and it lifted every benchmark at once.

BERT, from Google in 2018, is an encoder. It sees a whole sentence at once with attention flowing both ways. It is pretrained by masking about fifteen percent of the tokens and asking the model to fill them in, which forces it to use left and right context.
The result is a contextual embedding for every token: the vector for 'bank' differs by sentence. To classify, add a small head on top and fine-tune on a few thousand labelled examples.
Encoder models and their successors, such as RoBERTa and ModernBERT, remain the efficient workhorses for classification, tagging, search and embeddings.

lesson.code:
from transformers import pipeline, AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
clf = pipeline('sentiment-analysis')
print(clf('The plot was thin but the acting was wonderful.'))

gen = pipeline('text-generation', model='gpt2')
print(gen('Natural language processing is', max_new_tokens=20, do_sample=True, temperature=0.8))

items: GPT, from OpenAI, is a decoder. It reads left to right under a causal mask and is trained to predict the next token. That one simple goal, applied to a large part of the written internet, teaches grammar, facts, style and a lot of reasoning.

Scaling up gave GPT-2, GPT-3 and the line of large language models, including Llama and Claude. The surprise was in-context learning: show a big model a few examples in the prompt and it performs the task with no training.

A raw pretrained model continues text; it does not obey. Instruction tuning on prompt and answer pairs, then reinforcement learning from human feedback or similar preference methods, turns it into an assistant that follows requests and refuses harmful ones.

At generation time, sampling settings matter: temperature scales how adventurous choices are, and top-k or top-p keep only the likeliest tokens. Evaluation is hard, since open-ended answers have no single right text.
Later in your studies, a dedicated course on decision models looks at a new use of encoders and decoders: instead of writing text, answering fixed questions with calibrated probabilities in one pass.

practice.title: Temperature
practice.intro: Write apply_temperature(logits, T): the softmax of logits divided by T, rounded to 4 decimals.
practice.hint: Low T sharpens, high T flattens.
practice.solution:
import math
def apply_temperature(logits, T):
    scaled = [v / T for v in logits]
    m = max(scaled)
    e = [math.exp(v - m) for v in scaled]
    t = sum(e)
    return [round(v / t, 4) for v in e]

practice.title: Top-k filter
practice.intro: Write top_k(probs, k): keep the k largest probabilities (ties: lower index first), set the rest to 0 and renormalise; round to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
def top_k(probs, k):
    order = sorted(range(len(probs)), key=lambda i: (-probs[i], i))
    keep = set(order[:k])
    s = sum([probs[i] for i in keep])
    return [round(probs[i] / s, 4) if i in keep else 0 for i in range(len(probs))]

practice.title: Top-p (nucleus)
practice.intro: Write top_p(probs, p): sort probabilities descending (ties: lower index first) and keep the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p; set the others to 0 and renormalise; round to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
def top_p(probs, p):
    order = sorted(range(len(probs)), key=lambda i: (-probs[i], i))
    keep = []
    cum = 0.0
    for i in order:
        keep.append(i)
        cum = cum + probs[i]
        if cum >= p - 1e-12:
            break
    ks = set(keep)
    s = sum([probs[i] for i in ks])
    return [round(probs[i] / s, 4) if i in ks else 0 for i in range(len(probs))]

summary: Search engines use an inverted index to find documents containing query words and rank them with BM25, a refined TF-IDF. Modern systems add embedding-based dense retrieval and neural rerankers.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant passages and puts them in the prompt of a language model so its answer is grounded in sources.
Machine translation, summarisation and question answering are evaluated with overlap metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, and increasingly by human or model judges.
Responsible NLP means checking for hallucination, bias, privacy leaks and misuse, and testing on the people the system will serve.

glossary.def: A map from each word to the list of documents containing it.
A ranking function combining term frequency with saturation, length normalisation and IDF.
Retrieval-augmented generation: fetching documents and giving them to a model to ground its answer.
A translation metric measuring n-gram overlap between output and reference translations.
Fluent output that is not supported by the input or facts.

keyPoints: Inverted index: word -> document ids.
BM25 saturates term frequency.
RAG: retrieve, then generate.
Chunk long documents with overlap.
Check facts, bias and privacy.

items: ELI5. To answer a question about your school, first find the right pages in the handbook, then give the pages to a helper to answer from.

When you search a million pages you do not scan them. A search engine builds an inverted index in advance: for each word, the list of documents that contain it. A query is answered by looking up its words and intersecting or merging the lists. Then the candidates are ranked.
BM25 is the classic ranking function: like TF-IDF, but extra occurrences of a word count for less and less, and long documents are penalised gently.
Embeddings add meaning. Encode documents and queries as dense vectors with an encoder model and retrieve the nearest, so 'cheap flights' also finds 'low-cost airfare'.

Production search often combines the two, lexical and dense, and finishes with a reranker, a model that reads the query and each candidate together and scores them accurately. Quality is measured by precision at k, recall at k and mean reciprocal rank.

lesson.code:
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
corpus = [d.lower().split() for d in docs]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(corpus)
scores = bm25.get_scores('refund policy'.split())

# RAG skeleton
hits = retrieve(query, k=4)
context = '\n\n'.join(h.text for h in hits)
prompt = f'Answer using only the context.\n\nContext:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}'
answer = llm(prompt)

items: Large language models know a lot but can make things up and cannot know your private or recent documents. Retrieval-augmented generation fixes both: retrieve the relevant passages, paste them into the prompt, and instruct the model to answer from them and cite them.
Long documents are cut into overlapping chunks so that no answer is split across a boundary. Retrieval quality is usually the limit of such systems.

Other tasks have their own metrics. Machine translation systems are scored by BLEU, the overlap of n-grams with human reference translations, and summaries by ROUGE, which stresses recall. Overlap scores are crude, so human review and carefully validated model judges are used too.
Finally, responsibility: language models learn from human text and inherit its stereotypes, may leak private data, may state falsehoods with confidence and can be misused.
Test on the groups and languages your users speak, measure rather than assume, keep humans in the loop for high-stakes uses, and be open about limits.

practice.title: Build an inverted index
practice.intro: Write inverted_index(docs): docs is a list of token lists; return [word, sorted list of document ids containing it] pairs sorted by word.
practice.hint: Add each document to each word's list once.

practice.title: Boolean AND query
practice.intro: Write search_and(docs, words): the sorted ids of documents containing all the words.
practice.solution:
def search_and(docs, words):
    return [i for i in range(len(docs)) if all([w in docs[i] for w in words])]

practice.title: BM25 score
practice.intro: Write bm25(query, doc, docs, k1, b): the BM25 score of a token-list doc for the query tokens, using idf = ln((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1), the term-frequency part tf (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 (1 - b + b len(doc) / avgdl)), summed over query terms. Round to 4 decimals.
practice.solution:
import math
def bm25(query, doc, docs, k1, b):
    N = len(docs)
    avgdl = sum([len(d) for d in docs]) / float(N)
    s = 0.0
    for q in query:
        df = len([d for d in docs if q in d])
        idf = math.log((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1)
        tf = doc.count(q)
        s = s + idf * tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len(doc) / avgdl))
    return round(s, 4)

practice.title: Precision and recall at k
practice.intro: Write pr_at_k(ranked, relevant, k): [precision@k, recall@k] for a ranked list of ids and the set of relevant ids, each rounded to 3 decimals.
practice.hint: Count relevant items in the top k.
practice.solution:
def pr_at_k(ranked, relevant, k):
    top = ranked[:k]
    hit = len([d for d in top if d in relevant])
    return [round(hit / float(k), 3), round(hit / float(len(relevant)), 3)]

practice.title: Mean reciprocal rank
practice.intro: Write mrr(rankings, relevants): for each query, 1 / rank of the first relevant id in its ranking (0 if none); return the mean rounded to 3 decimals. rankings is a list of id lists and relevants a list of id lists.

practice.title: Chunk text
practice.intro: Write chunk(tokens, size, overlap): split the token list into windows of size tokens, each starting size - overlap after the previous one; stop when a window reaches the end.

practice.title: Unigram BLEU precision
practice.intro: Write unigram_precision(candidate, reference): the fraction of candidate tokens that appear in the reference, clipped by how many times each appears there, rounded to 3 decimals.
